NJ Senate Panel Advances Bill to Fine, Not Jail, Underage Gamblers

Published October 19, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A New Jersey Senate committee has advanced S597, a bipartisan bill sponsored by Sens. James Beach and Vincent Polistina that would stop treating underage casino gambling as a criminal matter. Under current law, gambling underage at a licensed New Jersey casino is a disorderly persons offense; S597 would replace that with a straightforward civil penalty instead.

How the fines would work

For a person under 21 caught entering or gambling at a licensed casino or simulcasting facility, the bill sets civil fines at $500 for a first violation, $1,000 for a second, and $2,000 for a third or subsequent violation. The bill doesn't stop at the minor, either — casino licensees, employees, and adults who knowingly allow someone under their care to gamble underage would also face penalties, though the specific dollar amounts for those parties weren't detailed in the reporting reviewed for this piece. Casino employees would retain a good-faith defense if they checked and reasonably relied on written proof of age that turned out to be false.

Where the fine money goes

Revenue collected under the bill would flow into the state's General Fund and then be appropriated to the Department of Human Services for compulsive gambling prevention, education, and treatment programs — tying the penalty structure directly to problem-gambling resources rather than general state revenue.

S597 covers licensed land-based casinos and simulcasting facilities specifically. Reporting on the bill did not describe it as extending to online sports betting or online casino accounts, so its scope as advanced appears to be in-person gambling.

Part of a broader push

This isn't the first attempt at this kind of change — a similar decriminalization proposal cleared a New Jersey Assembly committee back in late 2024 with the same fine structure, before stalling. The bill's reappearance this session, paired with a separate committee-advanced resolution this same week aimed at restricting gambling ads targeted at people showing signs of addiction, suggests state lawmakers are continuing to focus on the compliance and marketing side of New Jersey's gambling industry even as the underlying legal betting market keeps growing.

Why it matters

If S597 becomes law, it would mark a shift in how New Jersey treats underage gambling specifically — moving away from a criminal record for a first-time violation and toward a fine paired with funding for treatment programs. For the casino industry, it also keeps the compliance spotlight on age verification at the point of entry, an area regulators in multiple states have been tightening in 2026.
